title: GPU fleet & cloud accounts: IaC, CI/CD and runbook — implementation guide
author: Aisha Martinez
body:
Overview

This doc consolidates the operational implementation guidance for Redwood's GPU fleet and associated cloud accounts/networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines and primary runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who are responsible for provisioning, scaling, and operating GPU-backed inference capacity.

Scope

- Target components: GPU compute pools (hosted/dedicated), VPC/networking, cloud accounts and IAM, Terraform modules for fleet and networking, CI/CD build and deploy pipelines, and operational runbooks for common events.
- Out of scope: model runtime tuning, customer-facing API docs, and private deployment packaging details (see eng-private-deployments reference pages).

Goals

1. Provide repeatable IaC patterns for fleet and networking that meet security and compliance requirements.
2. Standardize CI/CD for safe, auditable infrastructure changes with automated preflight checks.
3. Define capacity planning and scaling playbooks to maintain SLOs.
4. Capture operational runbooks for common incidents (capacity shortage, network partition, failed Terraform apply).

High-level architecture and ownership

- GPU Fleet Controller (service: gpu-fleet-svc) — owned by eng-infra, primary contact: infra-platform team.
- IaC modules repo (git: infra-modules) — owned by infra-iac team.
- CI/CD pipelines (repo: infra-pipelines) — owned by infra-ci team.
- Cloud accounts & networking — cloud-accounts team (AWS/GCP accounts), security reviews via security-and-compliance.

SLOs and operational thresholds

- 95th percentile single-request latency (inference routing) — 300ms target for interactive routes.
- Fleet availability SLO: 99.9% per region for Dedicated pools.
- Autoscale target: maintain >= 15% spare GPU capacity headroom during business hours.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - GPU utilization > 85% for 5m -> Severity P2.
  - Pod pending due to Unschedulable for > 3m -> Severity P2.
  - Terraform drift detection (diff != 0) on prod infra -> Severity P1 if > 10 resources changed.

IaC modules & patterns (Terraform)

- Module layout: infra-modules/gpu_pool, infra-modules/networking, infra-modules/cloud_accounts, infra-modules/iam. Each module must have:
  - inputs.tf (required inputs), outputs.tf, examples/ (usage), README.md with security notes.
  - A versioned release pipeline that publishes tags and a registry entry.
- Best practices:
  - Use remote state per environment (backend: s3 + DynamoDB locking or GCS + locking), state prefixes: "redwood/{env}/{component}".
  - Keep resource counts and sizing in variables.tf with guarded validation blocks (min/max).
  - Separate mutable runtime resources (ASG, instance pools) from static networking resources.
  - Avoid dynamic for_each over unknown-length lists for core networking resources; prefer explicit counts with validations.

Example variables table (human-readable)

- name: gpu_instance_type — description: EC2/GCE instance shape (e.g., p4d.24xlarge / a2-megagpu) — default: p4d.
- name: gpu_count_min — description: Minimum GPUs in pool — default: "2"
- name: gpu_count_max — description: Maximum GPUs in pool — default: "200"
- name: autoscale_policy — description: pre-defined policy id for scaling behavior — default: "throughput-balanced"

Terraform deployment workflow (CI/CD)

1. Change proposal: all infra changes must be made via a pull request against the infra-modules or environment overlays repo.
2. Preflight checks (automated):
   - terraform fmt + validate
   - terraform init -backend-config=... (use ephemeral creds)
   - terratest/unit tests for module logic (if present)
   - static policy checks: Sentinel/Opa or terraform-compliance policies (IAM, public-s3, network egress)
   - cost-estimation: run cost-scan to detect large capacity increases
3. Plan stage: CI pipeline runs terraform plan with a workspace per environment and posts the plan to the PR.
4. Approval gates:
   - Small changes (<= 5 resources and no IAM/network changes): auto-approve by infra leads.
   - Large changes (resource count > 5, or any IAM/network change): require two approvers including one from security/cloud-accounts.
5. Apply:
   - Apply runs in the dedicated deploy pipeline using short-lived cloud service account credentials, with keepalives and logging to deploy audit.
   - Notify Slack #infra-deploys with plan summary and apply result.

CI/CD pipeline templates and example commands

- Pipeline stages (recommended): lint -> test -> plan -> gated-approval -> apply -> post-checks.
- Example CLI snippet (run locally or in CI agent):

  export TF_ENV=prod
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-terraform-state" -backend-config="key=redwood/prod/gpu_pool.tfstate"
  terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -out=plan.out
  terraform show -no-color plan.out > plan.txt

- Rollback guidance: use the last-known-good state snapshot; for complex changes, prefer a targeted inverse change (e.g., revert the PR) rather than state surgery.

Cloud accounts & networking

- Account structure: separate accounts per environment (dev, staging, prod) and per region for Dedicated pools requiring data isolation.
- Networking: VPC per account with standardized CIDR allocation. Peering/transit architecture must follow network-standards ADR.
- Security controls:
  - Centralized bastion and SSM jump hosts for management access.
  - Flow logs + VPC endpoint-only S3 access for state buckets.
  - Private subnets for GPU nodes, NAT/egress with strict allowlists.

CI/CD for build and image promotion

- GPU node images are built in infra-ci (packer/image-repo) and promoted through environments: base -> validated -> prod-ready.
- Image build checks: kernel compat, CUDA/cuDNN versions, container runtime tests, sidecar healthchecks.
- Tagging: images must include build metadata: git-sha, build-timestamp, image-signature.

Capacity planning and scaling playbook

- Monthly capacity planning cadence: infra-team-runbook meeting on first Monday of month to review usage trends and upcoming commitments.
- Inputs: 30/60/90 day forecast from product, historical GPU-hours, rolling growth rate.
- Provisioning lead times: cloud GPU quota increase requests often take 3-10 business days; include quota requests in forecast.

Autoscaling policies (recommended defaults)

- Throughput-balanced: scale based on average queued work per GPU over 2m window; cool-down 90s.
- Latency-priority: maintain spare capacity target 25% during business hours; aggressive scale-up, conservative scale-down.
- Cost-conservative: maintain headroom 5%, use burst pools that can be preemptible/spot.

Operational runbooks (common scenarios)

1) Capacity shortfall (alert: GPU utilization > 90% for > 10m)
   - Owner: oncall infra-sre.
   - Steps:
     1. Triage: check dashboards (Grafana: gpu-fleet-svc -> utilization, queue depth, pending pods).
     2. Verify if autoscaler is active: kubectl get hpa / check autoscaler logs.
     3. If autoscaler healthy but capacity saturated: trigger manual scale to +20% capacity via IaC overlay (create PR in overlays repo).
     4. If quota-limited: submit expedited quota increase to cloud-accounts and route traffic to fallback model variants (routing policy).
     5. Post-incident: update capacity forecast and run retrospective.

2) Failed Terraform apply (alert: apply failure in pipeline)
   - Owner: infra-iac.
   - Steps:
     1. Inspect plan and apply logs in CI; determine resource causing failure.
     2. If transient API error: retry apply with exponential backoff (pipeline supports retry).
     3. If change is destructive or unexpected: cancel pipeline, open a rollback PR, and notify stakeholders.
     4. If state inconsistency suspected: do not manually edit state without infra lead approval.

3) Network partition or cross-account connectivity failure
   - Owner: cloud-accounts/networking.
   - Steps:
     1. Validate route tables, NAT gateways, peering connections.
     2. Run diagnostic scripts (provided in repo: scripts/network-diagnostics.sh) which collect traceroutes and VPC flow logs.
     3. If critical, failover traffic to alternate region using smart routing and capacity pools.

Post-deploy checks and monitoring

- Always run smoke-tests against new capacity pools: health endpoint, KV cache warmup, and a small synthetic inference workload.
- Enable drift detection: daily terraform plan job that posts changes to audit channel. Significant drift should trigger a remediation PR.

Escalation and communication

- PagerDuty oncall rotations for infra-sre and infra-iac.
- Page on P1 events. Slack templates for incident comms are in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response.
- Every P1 incident requires a postmortem within 72 hours and a remediation plan assigned.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets

- Check state locking (AWS/Dynamo): aws dynamodb get-item --table-name tf-state-locks --key '{"LockID":{"S":"redwood/prod/gpu_pool.tfstate"}}'
- Terraform plan from CI agent (example): terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -input=false -out=plan.out
- Quick capacity increase (temporary): create overlay with gpu_count_min increased and submit PR to overlays repo with autoscaler set to manual.
